subject: penguin
pitch: An emperor penguin chick's proud parent. Glossy blue-black back and head, a crisp white belly blending into a warm golden-yellow patch at the neck and ear, a long slender beak with an orange-pink stripe, stubby flippers held slightly out, and big black feet. A fluffy grey chick peeks out from between its feet.
reasoning:
I'm planning the scene: an emperor penguin adult (~1.1 m) with a grey downy chick (~0.35 m) standing between its feet, using realistic proportions as a guide for the three.js model.

I need to structure the code around default export, imports from the builder SDK and three, and keep the model centered at x=0 facing +Z. For the creatures I'll build skeletons first with named joints and chains, separate upper/lower jaw parts, and use the part and paint functions (mottle, gradient, countershade) to add texture like the golden chest patch, all within the part/triangle/joint/color limits.

Now I'm working out the penguin's skeleton hierarchy, deciding where to anchor the root joint relative to the standing pose and feet placement.

I'm considering using a lathe to build the egg-shaped torso around the Y axis, then flattening it front-to-back with a scale option since penguins are compressed in that direction compared to a circular cross-section.

Actually, lathe can't be scaled directly, so I'm switching to a loft instead, building the body from stations along a vertical spine path with independent width and height values at each point to get the flattened oval shape. I'm working out how the loft's frame orientation behaves for a straight vertical path, tracing through the math to figure out which local axis ends up facing front versus back so I place the width and depth correctly.

For a vertical path without explicit up vector, parallel transport should keep the normal stable along -Z, so that should be fine even with slight path tilts. I'm also considering a simpler approach: using a scaled sphere geometry as an ellipsoid via the part's scale option, since part() applies scale through the mesh's transform matrix rather than the geometry itself, which should give a clean body shape.

Non-uniform scaling works fine in three.js since it correctly computes normal matrices, and skinning and paint-based coloring both work through the world transform matrix that includes scale. For the actual coloring, I'm planning to use a position/normal-based paint function distinguishing the dark blue-black back, white belly, and golden neck/ear patches characteristic of an emperor penguin, based on thresholds on the z-normal and y-position.

I'm refining the color zones further: blue-black for the back and head, white for the belly on the front, and a golden patch near the ears that blends into the chest, using smooth distance-based masking around the ear region and a mix function to blend colors between zones.

I'm also sketching out the overall body proportions for an adult emperor penguin—roughly 1.1m tall, with the head near the top, shoulders around 0.95, and the torso width tapering toward the belly—to anchor where these color transitions should fall on the model.

For the legs and feet, I'm noting penguins have very short legs mostly hidden in the body, with black webbed feet visible at the base providing the only ground contact.

For the torso shape itself, I'm weighing a stacked-ellipsoid approach versus a lofted form built from vertical stations between the hips and neck, leaning toward the loft for a smoother, more natural silhouette.

I'm sketching out a loft with four vertical stations tapering from wide at the belly to narrower at the shoulders and head, using a circular cross-section with enough sides to keep it smooth without looking too dense — settling on around 12 sides as a balance between low-poly charm and roundness. I'm also second-guessing whether a perfectly vertical collinear path will cause frame/normal issues in the sweep, since the tangent direction stays constant throughout, so I need to check how the orientation logic handles that degenerate case.

I'm thinking the body's bottom cap sits just above the ground near the feet, giving an egg-ish silhouette, and considering whether to simplify by using scaled spheres for the body/head instead. For the overall penguin, I'm sketching a plan: lofted body, ellipsoid head, a sweep-based beak, small spherical eyes, slab flippers and feet with toes, and for the fluffy grey chick I'm weighing whether to fake texture with cards or clusters of tiny spheres.

For the chick's fluffiness I'll avoid risky svg-fuzz textures and instead rely on overlapping grey/white mottled spheres plus a few cone-shaped tufts for a simple, safe stylized look. Now I'm setting up the overall coordinate system — penguin facing +Z, left side at +X, beak pointing forward — and starting the skeleton with a root joint placed at the ground center.

Working out the joint hierarchy: placing the hips as root around (0, 0.36, 0), then building a spine chain running upward through chest and neck using a curved path with a couple of named joints, making sure all joint names follow valid naming rules.

I decide it's cleaner to manually define each spine joint rather than rely on auto-generated chain names — hips, chest, neck, head, and a jaw joint at the head with a hinge. Then I turn to the legs, planning a short leg chain per side (hip to ankle/toe) to match a penguin's stubby proportions.

For each leg, I'm setting up a two-point polyline chain with named joints so the hip sits as the span joint and the ankle as the tip, keeping orientation so the foot can later be attached facing forward at the tip joint despite its downward-pointing axis.

For the feet, I'm defining a webbed foot outline as an extruded flat shape in the horizontal plane, orienting the extrude axes so forward maps to z and lateral spread maps to x, then laying out heel and three spreading toe points to form the foot silhouette.

I realize I can bind the extrude's `at` to the ankle joint so the foot outline positions relative to it, with the bone weighting rigidly attached to that joint. I need to offset the plane's y so the foot sits flat on the ground rather than at ankle height, using an explicit literal point for `at` alongside the bone reference.

For the legs themselves, since penguin legs are mostly hidden inside the body, I'm planning a thin black rod connecting hip to ankle to suggest the visible shank, then working out the body's loft profile stations from bottom to top with their widths.

Mapping out the emperor penguin silhouette: narrow neck, widest at chest around y=0.5, tapering back in at the shoulders, with a round top cap that gets covered by the head sphere positioned to overlap seamlessly. I'm sizing the head radius so it blends into the body's rounded cap at the top.
